unit-phys-dyn1-hooke.title: Dynamics 1 · 1-5 Hooke’s Law and the Spring Lab

summary.text: Hooke’s law, F = −kx, and the spring lab built on it: recording the stretch rather than the length, turning each hanging mass (hanger included) into a weight in newtons, reading the spring constant from the slope of a force–stretch graph, what the y-intercept and the percent error say about the data, and using the line to predict a force or a mass. Plus the lab’s own question: what changes on the Moon.

why.text: Springs are the cleanest example of a force that depends on position, and the lab is the first time you build a law from your own data instead of reading it off the sheet. The graph skills — slope, intercept, what a line through the origin means — come back in every lab after this one.

objectives.text: Determine the relationship between force and stretch for a vertical spring.
Find a spring constant from the slope of a force–stretch graph, with its units.
Use F = kx to predict the force for a stretch and the mass needed for a stretch, converting units first.
Explain why the spring constant does not change on the Moon even though the weights and stretches do.
Recognise the elastic limit, beyond which Hooke’s law no longer holds.

parentNote.text: From the class’s Hooke’s Law Lab sheet and entry 11 of her equation sheet (F = −kx). The lab has no data yet, so nothing here invents her readings: the unit teaches the reasoning behind each step and answers the lab’s own questions with fresh numbers (never the sheet’s 10 inches or 30 cm). The PhET part of the lab is done on her laptop and is not reproduced here. The traps with the most airtime: recording the length instead of the stretch, leaving the mass hanger out of the weight, grams or centimetres used without converting, a force in newtons treated as a mass, and the Moon — the weights and stretches shrink but the slope k does not. Three things on the sheets are worth a word with her teacher. The lab asks for a stretch of 10 inches while the class works in SI, so a card gives 1 in = 2.54 cm. The lab does not say which axis force goes on; the unit uses force on the vertical axis (slope = k) and says that the other way round gives 1/k, and every graded stem names its axes. And her sheet’s percent error, |b| ÷ y_max × 100, does not define b or y_max; in a lab that asks for slope, y-intercept and % error together it is taught as the intercept compared with the largest force, flagged as our reading. The elastic limit is added (the sheets only hint at it). The graphs here are real force–stretch plots, which the app draws properly, unlike free-body diagrams.

nextUp.text: Before the lab, learn the stretch-not-length and hanger cards. After it, use the Moon and backward-to-a-mass questions to check your conclusion and questions.

cards.def:
**The force a spring exerts is proportional to how far it is stretched or compressed.**
• Twice the stretch, twice the force — as long as the spring is not overstretched.
• It is entry 11 on your sheet.
cards.hint: Pull twice as far, it pulls back twice as hard.

cards.def:
**The minus sign says the spring’s force points the opposite way to its stretch or squash: always back toward its relaxed length.**
• Pull it down and it pulls up. Squash it and it pushes out.
• That is why it is called a restoring force. For the SIZE of the force, use kx and say the direction in words.
cards.hint: Stretch one way, force the other.

cards.def:
**x is the stretch — how much LONGER the spring got — not how long the spring is.**
• Stretch = loaded length − relaxed length.
• Measure the relaxed length first, with nothing hanging, then subtract it from every loaded reading.
• Your lab sheet puts this in capitals for a reason: using the length is the commonest way to ruin the whole graph.
cards.hint: The meter stick reads a length. You record a difference.

cards.def:
**The force on the spring is the weight of EVERYTHING hanging from it, F_g = mg, in newtons.**
• That includes the mass hanger itself, not just the slotted masses on it.
• Use 9.8 m/s² for the size of g; the force points down.

**Divide grams by 1000 before multiplying by g — a 250 g mass is 0.250 kg and weighs 2.45 N.**
• Multiplying grams straight by 9.8 makes every force a thousand times too big.
• A mass in grams is never a force in newtons, however tidy the number looks.

**k says how stiff a spring is: the force needed for each metre of stretch, in newtons per metre (N/m).**
• Bigger k, stiffer spring: more force for the same stretch.
• k belongs to the spring. It does not change with the masses you hang or the planet you are on.
cards.hint: Newtons per metre: force per stretch.

cards.term: What you choose and what you measure
cards.def:
**In this lab you choose the force (by choosing the masses), so force is the independent variable and stretch is the dependent one.**
• The spring decides the stretch; you read it off the meter stick.
• The spring constant is not a variable here at all — it is what the graph lets you find.

cards.term: The force–stretch graph: its slope is k
cards.def:
**With force on the vertical axis and stretch (in metres) on the horizontal, the slope of the best-fit line is the spring constant.**
• Slope = rise ÷ run = force ÷ stretch = k, in N/m.
• If your class puts stretch on the vertical axis instead, the slope is 1/k, in m/N — check which way your teacher wants it.
• The line on this card has a slope of 20 N/m.

cards.term: Why the line should go through the origin
cards.def:
**No weight hung, no stretch: an unloaded spring sits at its relaxed length, so the line should pass through (0, 0).**
• That is also why Hooke’s law has no "+ b" in it.

cards.term: An intercept that is not zero
cards.def:
**A best-fit line that clearly misses the origin points to a slip made the same way in every reading.**
• Leaving the hanger out of every weight drops every force by the hanger’s weight, so the line crosses the force axis BELOW zero.
• Recording lengths instead of stretches shifts every reading by the relaxed length.
• A small intercept is just scatter. A big one is a clue.

**Your sheet’s percent error is |b| ÷ y_max × 100 — in this lab, most likely the size of the y-intercept compared with the largest force you plotted.**
• It measures how far your line misses the origin, as a percentage.
• The sheet does not say what b and y_max are, so ask your teacher; this is the reading that fits a lab that asks for slope, y-intercept and % error together.

**On a force–stretch graph, the stiffer spring has the steeper line.**
• Steeper means more force for each centimetre of stretch.
• On this card, spring A (40 N/m) is four times as stiff as spring B (10 N/m).

**Your mathematical expression is the line’s equation with your own numbers in it: F = (your k) × x.**
• Use it forwards: put in a stretch, get a force.
• Use it backwards: put in a force, get a stretch.
• Keep the units on the slope, N/m, so the expression says what it means.

**To find the mass that gives a certain stretch: F = kx for the force, then m = F ÷ g for the mass.**
• Two steps, and the second one is the one people forget: a force in newtons is not a mass in kilograms.
• This is also how the PhET simulation’s unknown masses are found.

**1 inch is 2.54 cm, which is 0.0254 m — convert to metres before using k in N/m.**
• N/m only works with metres. A stretch in inches or centimetres has to be converted first, or the answer comes out tens or hundreds of times too big.

**Same masses on the Moon: smaller weights, so smaller stretches — but the same slope, because k belongs to the spring.**
• Independent values (the weights): smaller, about one-sixth, since g is about 1.6 m/s² there.
• Dependent values (the stretches): smaller by the same factor.
• Slope (k): unchanged. Every point slides down the SAME line toward the origin.
cards.hint: The spring does not know which planet it is on.

cards.def:
**Hooke’s law only holds up to the spring’s elastic limit; stretched past it, the line bends and the spring stays longer for good.**
• On the graph, the points stop following the straight line.
• A damaged spring never returns to its relaxed length, so its readings no longer count.

cards.term: Why one trial is enough here
cards.def:
**A hanging mass that has stopped moving gives the same stretch every time, so this lab needs one careful reading per mass, not several trials.**
• Wait for the bouncing to stop before you read the meter stick.
• Read the scale at eye level, at the same point on the spring each time.

questions.q: In your sheet’s Hooke’s law, F = −kx, what does the minus sign tell you?
opts: The spring’s force points opposite to its stretch or squash
The spring constant is negative whenever a spring is stretched
The force gets weaker the further the spring is pulled out
The spring’s force is always smaller than the weight it holds
questions.hint: Pull a spring down. Which way does it pull?
steps: Stretch a spring downward and it pulls back up.
Squash it and it pushes back out.
Either way, its force is opposite to its displacement x.
The minus sign records exactly that: the force is a restoring force.

ex.main: **The minus sign shows the spring always pulls or pushes back toward its relaxed length — opposite to x.** k itself is always positive, and the size of the force, kx, grows with the stretch rather than shrinking.
ex.tip: For the size use kx; for the direction say "back toward relaxed".

questions.q: A spring hangs from a clamp. A hand pulls its lower end 6 cm below its relaxed position and holds it there. Which way does the spring pull on the hand?
opts: Down, the same way it was stretched
Up, back toward its relaxed length
Sideways, at right angles to the stretch
Neither way, until the hand lets go
questions.hint: It is a restoring force.
steps: The spring has been stretched downward.
A spring’s force is opposite to its stretch.
So it pulls upward on whatever is holding its end.
It pulls up, toward its relaxed length.

ex.main: **Stretched down, the spring pulls up — that is the minus sign in F = −kx.** It pulls the whole time it is stretched, not only once it is released; the hand can feel it.
ex.tip: Stretch down, pull up.

questions.q: What are the units of a spring constant?
opts: m/N
N·m
N/m
kg/m
questions.hint: k = F ÷ x.
steps: k is force divided by stretch.
Force is in newtons and stretch is in metres.
So k is newtons divided by metres.
The unit is N/m.

ex.main: **k = F ÷ x, so its unit is newtons per metre, N/m.** m/N is the ratio upside down, which is what the slope would be with stretch on the vertical axis; N·m multiplies instead of dividing; and kg/m mixes up mass and force.
ex.tip: Force per stretch: N/m.

questions.q: In a spring lab where you hang chosen masses and measure how far the spring stretches, what is the independent variable?
opts: The length of the spring before loading
The stretch you read off the meter stick
The spring constant of the spring itself
The weight hung, set by the masses you choose
questions.hint: Which one do YOU decide?
steps: The independent variable is the one you choose and change.
You decide which masses to hang, so you set the weight.
The spring then decides the stretch, which you measure.
So the weight is independent and the stretch is dependent.

ex.main: **You choose the masses, so the weight (the force) is the independent variable; the stretch is what you measure.** The spring constant is what the experiment finds, and the relaxed length is a starting point you subtract, not a variable.
ex.tip: Chosen = independent. Measured = dependent.

questions.q: Why should a spring’s force-against-stretch line pass through the origin?
opts: With no weight hung, the spring sits at its relaxed length
Every straight line drawn on a graph has to start at zero
The meter stick starts at zero, so the readings must too
The spring constant stays at zero until a mass is hung
questions.hint: What is the stretch when the force is zero?
steps: With nothing pulling on it, a spring is at its relaxed length.
Its stretch is then zero.
Zero force and zero stretch is the point (0, 0).
So the line should pass through the origin.

ex.main: **Zero force means zero stretch, so (0, 0) is a real data point.** Plenty of straight lines miss the origin; this one should not, which is why a big intercept on your graph is worth explaining.
ex.tip: No pull, no stretch.

questions.q: A 350 g mass hangs from a spring. What force does it pull down with, in newtons?
questions.hint: Grams to kilograms first, then F_g = mg.
steps: The mass pulls down on the spring with 3.43 N.

ex.main: **350 g = 0.350 kg, and 0.350 × 9.8 = 3.43 N.** 350 N treats grams as newtons, 0.35 N treats kilograms as newtons, and 3430 N multiplies the grams by 9.8 without converting.
ex.tip: Divide by 1000, then multiply by 9.8.

questions.q: A spring is 12.0 cm long with nothing on it. With 0.150 kg hanging from it (hanger included) it is 19.0 cm long. What is its spring constant?
opts: 21 N/m
questions.hint: x is the stretch, not the length.
steps: Stretch: 19.0 cm − 12.0 cm = 7.0 cm = 0.070 m.

ex.main: **k = 1.47 N ÷ 0.070 m = 21 N/m.** 7.7 N/m divides by the whole 19.0 cm length instead of the 7.0 cm stretch — the mistake the lab sheet warns about in capitals. 0.21 N/m leaves the stretch in centimetres, and 2140 N/m uses the 150 grams as if they were newtons.
ex.tip: Subtract the relaxed length first. Always.

questions.q: A 50 g mass hanger carrying 150 g of slotted masses stretches a spring 8.0 cm. What is the spring constant?
questions.hint: Everything hanging from the spring pulls on it.
steps: Total mass hanging: 50 g + 150 g = 200 g = 0.200 kg.
Stretch: 8.0 cm = 0.080 m.

ex.main: **The hanger counts: 0.200 kg weighs 1.96 N, and 1.96 ÷ 0.080 = 24.5 N/m.** 18.4 N/m leaves the hanger out, 0.245 N/m keeps the stretch in centimetres, and 2500 N/m uses the 200 grams as newtons.
ex.tip: Hanger + masses, in kilograms, times 9.8.

questions.q: The graph shown plots the force on a spring in newtons (vertical axis) against its stretch in metres (horizontal axis). What is the spring constant?
opts: 16 N/m
questions.hint: The slope is rise over run.
steps: Pick a point on the line far from the origin: (0.25 m, 4.0 N).
The line starts at (0, 0), so the rise is 4.0 N and the run is 0.25 m.

ex.main: **The slope is 4.0 N ÷ 0.25 m = 16 N/m.** 4.0 N/m reads one force off the graph and calls it k; 0.063 N/m divides the stretch by the force; and 0.16 N/m treats the 0.25 m as 25.
ex.tip: Slope of force against stretch = k.

questions.q: The graph shown plots force against stretch for two springs, A and B. Which statement is true?
opts: B is stiffer: it stretches further for the same force
A is stiffer: it needs more force per metre of stretch
A is stiffer: it stretches further for the same force
They are equally stiff: both lines start from zero
questions.hint: Steeper line, more force per metre.
steps: The slope of each line is its spring constant k.
A’s line is steeper: 30 N/m against B’s 12 N/m.
A bigger k means more force for each metre of stretch.
So A is the stiffer spring, and it stretches LESS for the same force.

ex.main: **A’s steeper line means a bigger k, so A is stiffer and stretches less for any given force.** Stretching further for the same force is what makes B the softer one. Starting at zero says nothing about stiffness: every ideal spring’s line does.
ex.tip: Stiffer = steeper.

questions.q: A spring has a spring constant of 36 N/m. How much force does it exert when it is stretched 18 cm?
questions.hint: Centimetres to metres, then F = kx.
steps: It pulls back toward its relaxed length with 6.48 N.

ex.main: **F = kx = 36 N/m × 0.18 m = 6.48 N.** 648 N uses 18 as metres, 200 N divides k by the stretch, and 0.005 N divides the stretch by k.
ex.tip: N/m needs metres.

questions.q: A spring has a spring constant of 42 N/m. What mass would you hang on it to stretch it 6.0 inches? (1 inch = 2.54 cm)
opts: 6.4 kg
questions.hint: Inches to metres, F = kx, then m = F ÷ g.

ex.main: **6.0 in is 0.1524 m, so F = 42 × 0.1524 = 6.40 N and m = 6.40 ÷ 9.8 = 0.65 kg.** 25.7 kg uses the 6.0 inches as if they were metres, 65.3 kg uses the 15.24 centimetres as metres, and 6.4 kg stops at the force and calls newtons kilograms.
ex.tip: Convert, multiply by k, divide by g.

questions.q: A 2.0 N weight stretches a spring 3.0 cm. Without passing the elastic limit, how far will a 5.0 N weight stretch it?
opts: 7.5 cm
1.2 cm
15 cm
6.0 cm
questions.hint: Stretch is proportional to force.
steps: The force goes from 2.0 N to 5.0 N: 5.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.5 times as much.
Hooke’s law says the stretch grows by the same factor.
The stretch is 7.5 cm.

ex.main: **Two and a half times the force gives two and a half times the stretch: 7.5 cm.** 1.2 cm flips the ratio, 15 cm multiplies by 5 instead of by 2.5, and 6.0 cm adds a centimetre per newton, which only happens for a spring with k = 100 N/m — not this one.
ex.tip: Same factor for force and stretch.

questions.q: A spring lab is repeated on the Moon with the same masses. What happens to the weights hung (the independent values) and to the stretches (the dependent values)?
opts: The weights get smaller, but the stretches stay put
Both get smaller: lighter weights stretch it less
The weights stay put, but the stretches get smaller
Both stay the same, because the masses are the same
questions.hint: Same mass, smaller g.
steps: Weight is mg, and g on the Moon is about 1.6 m/s² instead of 9.8.
So each mass weighs about one-sixth as much there.
A smaller force stretches the same spring less, by the same factor.
Both the weights and the stretches get smaller.

ex.main: **The masses are the same, but each weighs about a sixth as much, so every stretch is about a sixth as big too.** "The masses are the same" is true and is exactly the trap: the spring responds to weight, not mass.
ex.tip: Same masses, smaller weights, smaller stretches.

questions.q: A spring lab is repeated on the Moon with the same masses, and force is graphed on the vertical axis against stretch on the horizontal. What happens to the slope of the line?
opts: It rises, because the spring now stretches less
It drops to about a sixth, just as the weights do
It stays the same, because k belongs to the spring
It drops to zero, because the weights barely count
questions.hint: What does the slope measure?
steps: The slope of force against stretch is k.
On the Moon the forces and the stretches both shrink by the same factor.
Force ÷ stretch is therefore unchanged.
The slope stays the same: every point slides down the same line.

ex.main: **The slope is k, a property of the spring, so it does not change; the points just sit closer to the origin on the same line.** Weights shrink, stretches shrink with them, and their ratio holds steady. g never appears in k.
ex.tip: The spring does not know which planet it is on.

questions.q: On the Moon, where g is about 1.6 m/s², a 0.30 kg mass hangs from a spring with a spring constant of 8.0 N/m. How far does it stretch the spring?
opts: 3.8 cm
6.0 cm
questions.hint: Moon weight first, then x = F ÷ k.
steps: Weight on the Moon: 0.30 × 1.6 = 0.48 N.
It stretches 6.0 cm.

ex.main: **F = 0.30 × 1.6 = 0.48 N, and x = 0.48 ÷ 8.0 = 0.060 m = 6.0 cm.** 36.8 cm uses Earth’s 9.8, 3.8 cm divides the mass by k as if kilograms were newtons, and 0.060 cm forgets to turn metres into centimetres.
ex.tip: k stays 8.0 N/m on the Moon. Only the weight changes.

questions.q: A best-fit line of force against stretch crosses the force axis at −0.49 N instead of passing through zero. Which slip, made in every reading, would produce exactly that?
opts: Leaving a 50 g hanger out of every weight
Writing every stretch in cm instead of m
Using 10 m/s² for g instead of 9.8 m/s²
Running each reading three times, not once
questions.hint: Which slip shifts every force by the same amount?
steps: A slip that shifts every force down by the same amount moves the whole line down.
A 50 g hanger weighs 0.050 × 9.8 = 0.49 N.
Leaving it out makes every force 0.49 N too small.
The line then crosses the force axis at −0.49 N.

ex.main: **Forgetting the hanger lowers every force by its 0.49 N weight, which drops the whole line by 0.49 N.** Centimetres instead of metres changes the slope, not the intercept; using 10 for g scales every force a little, which also changes only the slope; and extra trials just average the same values.
ex.tip: Same shift in every reading = an intercept.

questions.q: Your sheet gives percent error as |b| ÷ y_max × 100. A spring graph’s best-fit line has a y-intercept b of −0.18 N, and the largest force plotted, y_max, is 6.0 N. What is the percent error?
questions.hint: Drop the sign, divide, multiply by 100.
steps: The percent error is 3.0%.

ex.main: **|−0.18| ÷ 6.0 × 100 = 3.0%.** 0.030% puts a % sign on the fraction without ever multiplying by 100, 3333% divides the wrong way round, and −3.0% keeps the sign the absolute-value bars remove.
ex.tip: The bars make it positive; ×100 makes it a percent.

questions.q: A student keeps adding masses to a spring. After a certain point each new 0.5 N of weight stretches it much further than before, and once the masses come off it stays longer than it started. What happened?
opts: Hooke’s law still holds there; only the meter stick reading is off
Its spring constant went up, so each weight stretches it further
It went past its elastic limit and is now permanently stretched
It ran out of stretch, and will snap back fully once it is unloaded
questions.hint: Does it go back to its relaxed length?
steps: Hooke’s law only holds up to the elastic limit.
Past it, equal steps of force stop giving equal steps of stretch.
A spring stretched that far does not return to its relaxed length.
It has passed its elastic limit and been permanently deformed.

ex.main: **The straight line ended at the elastic limit; past it the spring deformed for good.** A bigger k would mean LESS stretch per newton, not more, and a spring that stays longer has plainly not snapped back.
ex.tip: Straight line only up to the elastic limit.

questions.q: Rank these springs from STIFFEST to SOFTEST.
opts: Spring B: 4.0 N stretches it 5.0 cm
Spring A: 4.2 N stretches it 7.0 cm
Spring C: 7.5 N stretches it 25 cm
Spring D: 2.0 N stretches it 20 cm
questions.hint: Work out k = F ÷ x for each, in N/m.

ex.main: **Stiffness is force per stretch: B 80 N/m, A 60 N/m, C 30 N/m, D 10 N/m.** Spring C carries the biggest force, but it needed a long stretch to get there, so it is only third. The force alone never tells you how stiff a spring is.
ex.tip: Compare k, not the force.

sorts.title: Move the spring lab to the Moon

items.t: The weight of each hanging mass
items.why: Weight is mg, and g is about a sixth as big there.
A smaller weight stretches the same spring less.

items.t: The largest force on your graph
items.why: The heaviest mass weighs less there, so the top force is smaller.

items.t: The mass needed to stretch the spring 5 cm
items.why: The same force needs about six times the mass when g is a sixth as big.

items.t: How far the empty hanger stretches the spring
items.why: The hanger weighs less there too.

items.t: The meter stick reading for each mass
items.why: Smaller stretches leave the end of the spring at a different mark.
Mass is the amount of matter; it is the same everywhere.
k belongs to the spring. g never appears in it.

items.t: The slope of force against stretch
items.why: The slope is k, and forces and stretches shrink together.

items.t: The force needed to stretch the spring 5 cm
items.why: F = kx, and neither k nor x has changed. Only the mass that supplies it would.

items.t: The mass of the empty hanger, in grams
items.why: A hanger is the same amount of metal wherever it is. Only its weight shrinks.

items.t: The units of k, newtons per metre
items.why: Units are units, on any planet.
